Not that I'm disagreeing with you I'd just like to hear you elaborate a little more if you have the time.

I'll use some numbers from memory to save me looking up US tax code for an hour to get exact percentages:

1) Capital gains tax rates are %18. So if you buy $1000 in stocks and sell them for $1100, you pay 18% of that gain in taxes - or $18 in taxes, $82 in net profits for you to keep. But if you sell those stocks at a loss because the market is down (like it has been for the last year or so), you pay no taxes because you made no profit. You also pay no taxes if you hold the stocks for a long time, which is what you /should/ do if you're a savvy investor. Day trading is gambling.

2) An asset tax would lead to your $1000 in stock being taxed to the tune of e.g. 5% a year. This is a problem for stocks, and devastating for bonds where the return will never be high enough to offset the taxes unless you're buying junk bonds (Greece anyone?) and you get lucky and they don't default (good luck). Asset taxes leads to capital flight as we've seen in e.g. Cyprus because everyone with assets moves them out of the country to avoid taxation (why keep your investments in the US where you guarantee at least e.g. a 5% decrease in value per year when you could move them anywhere else and avoid that?)

3) This is even more of an issue for illiquid assets. E.g. I can sell 5% of my stock per year to pay an asset tax. But how do I sell 5% of a power plant? Chop off a smoke stack?
